subject: latent growth model binary variable error "Could not compute standard errors"

messages.author: d68921926556beaf
messages.subject: latent growth model binary variable error "Could not compute standard errors"
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to examine the relationship between changes in a binary variable(supervisor status coded 0 and 1) and changes in a continuous variable (Job demand).
So I want to examine whether becoming a supervisor from a non-supervisor or becoming a non-supervisor from a supervisor has an influence on changes in job demands over time.

I wanted to see if lavaan can examine this relationship with made up data I created with 10 items which I've attached.

Syntax I used:

model <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i1 =~ 1*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 1*JD3
    s1 =~ 0*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 2*JD3
   
     i2 =~ 1*SS1 + 1*SS2 + 1*SS3
    s2 =~ 0*SS1 + 1*SS2 + 2*SS3
   
    s1 ~ s2
'
fit <- growth(model, data = diss
              #ordered=c("SS1", "SS2", "SS3")
)
summary(fit)

Error message I received:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
2: In lav_test_satorra_bentler(lavobject = NULL, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not invert information matrix needed for robust test statistic

3: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative
4: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables
                is not positive definite;
                use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv") to investigate.

I believe the first error message is the main problem and rest are due to made up data.
I searched this group to find a resolution and found this link.
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/mfR2zqXCEgU/BnI2N_J7AwAJ

I tried to delete " i2 =~ 1*SS1 + 1*SS2 + 1*SS3" which I believe free estimates of intercepts, and ran the command again but I run into same error.
I would greatly appreciate it if I could get some assistance!
Thank you so much.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: latent growth model binary variable error "Could not compute standard errors"
parts: I believe the first error message is the main problem and rest are due to made up data.
Try simulating more than N = 10 data points (like N = 500).  That will become especially necessary when you treat the binary data appropriately as ordered.

I searched this group to find a resolution and found this link.
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/mfR2zqXCEgU/BnI2N_J7AwAJ
Did you read the paper?  When you treat the data as binary, you will need to fix the thresholds to zero in your syntax.
I tried to delete " i2 =~ 1*SS1 + 1*SS2 + 1*SS3" which I believe free estimates of intercepts

No, you didn't specify any intercepts; that syntax fixes the loadings to 1.  The growth() wrapper will fix your intercepts to zero by default.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

So if I understand correctly, when the data is binary, I need to fix the thresholds to zero, but the growth() wrapper fix my intercepts to zero by default.
So I don't need to do anything in my syntax to fix the threshold.
In other words, my syntax is correct, and I just need to try running the code with more data (N=500).
Did I understand your response correctly?

Also, another question is that do I need to order the binary variables in the code (ordered=c("SS1", "SS2", "SS3"))?
I learned that binary variables can be treated like continuous numeric variables in latent growth model, because binary variables have only two values, they have only one difference, and it has to be equal to itself. This is not true for categorical variables because the difference between 1 and 2 can be different from the difference between 2 and 3 in categorical variables. Can I just treat binary variables same as continuous variable if I use the growth() function, which fix my intercepts to zero by default?

I created the other post thinking this post was lost with other new ones without any response. I will delete it.


Thank you.

Best,

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: latent growth model binary variable error "Could not compute standard errors"
parts:
Michelle,
Thresholds and intercepts are distinct parameters in the model, not two words for the same thing.  If you have not already, I strongly recommend some introductory reading on categorical data in SEM.  There is a lot to be aware of and it is not something you want to try to pick up on the fly.  A good SEM text is helpful to have at hand when toubleshooting an analysis.

You are working with a complex model.  For learning purposes, I would suggest that you first practice with simpler models, such as a growth curve with continuous variables, a path model with ordinal indicators, before trying to put all the elements together into one model.  That way, you can better isolate problems and see how things work in with fewer moving parts.

A very good strategy is to first write out the model you want to fit (or draw it with all parameters labeled).  Then write the syntax.  Then use the lavaanify() function to view the resulting parameter table.  Finally, check the table against your model to match up all the parameters.  If you prefer to see the parameters in their matrices, use lavInspect() with what='free'.  It is helpful to compare this to a parameter table at least once.

When you declare a variable as ordinal, at least two things happen.  First, the model is augmented to include a new latent continuous variable specific to that observed variable and a threshold model that relates the observed variable to the latent continuous variable through a set of cut points at which the continuous variable is broken into categories (just one threshold for dichotomous variables).  Second, the estimation procedure changes from something like maximum likelihood to something like diagonally weighted least squares.

Exogenous variables do not need to be declared ordinal because the rest of the model can be estimated conditional upon exogenous variables, and they are thus free of the normality assumption required for maximum-likelihood type estimators.  Endogenous variables need to be declared ordinal because they will violate this assumption.  Diagonally weighted least square is a computationally less intensive cousin of asymptotically distribution free estimation that allows you to estimate the parameters without the normality assumption when using thresholds for ordinal variables.  This comes at the cost of larger sample size requirements.

The assumption of equal intervals has more to do with the interpretation of the effect parameters in linear models.  The slope tells you how much y is expected to change for any unit change in x.  This is a single values assumed to hold for all values of x (e.g., a change from 1 to 2 as well as a change from 2 to 3).  This constancy of effect is implausible if the change from 1 to 2 does not represent the same amount of change in x as the change from 2 to 3.  Dummy coding essentially lets you estimate separate slopes for different pairs of values of x.

Finally, if you are not doing so already, consider using the simulateData() function to simulate your data from a model expressed in lavaan syntax.  If you do that, it forces you to specify every parameter in syntax.  You can then work backwards by removing some of the specified values to create model syntax for fitting the model with some parameters set free.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
